system.name: Barline
system.lead: Barline writes down what changes and leaves out what you already know. It never names an ingredient — the ingredient line does that. What is left is quantity, order and service, which turns out to be all a code needs to carry.

principles.t: Ingredients read top to bottom, base spirit first, and the code reads left to right in the same order. Position is the only thing binding a number to a bottle, so the two are never reordered apart.
A bare number is ounces beside a spirit and dashes beside bitters. Nothing marks which, because the bottle already told you. Same reason `r` is a rinse in an amount slot and a glass at the end.

principles.h: Case does the work of extra letters
principles.t: Rather than invent a second letter, one initial carries both halves of a pair — so there is less to memorise, not more. Where two garnishes want the same letter, lowercase is the one you reach for more often: `l` lemon, `L` lime; `s` sugar, `S` salt; `o` orange, `O` olive. Where it is a matter of degree, uppercase is the larger: `q` a quarter, `Q` three quarters; `r` a bare rocks glass, `R` one with ice.
Glass first, then whatever garnishes it, packed together and read as one word rather than letter by letter. `ccin` is a coupe with grated cinnamon, not `c` and `i` and `n`.
Egg white carries no measure because there is only one sensible amount, and a number there would be noise. Anything the drink assumes, the code leaves out.

system.footnote: The nearest relative is figured bass, where a composer writes the bass note and a few numbers for the intervals above it and the player fills in the harmony from what they already know. Same bargain: write the figures, trust the reader.

note: The house shorthand. Codes read left to right in build order, base spirit first, and end with one token for glass plus garnish. Everything is contextual — a bare number is ounces next to a spirit and dashes next to bitters.
